title: Compare and Contrast Security Implications of Different Architecture Models

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Organizations can build technology environments with cloud services, on-premises infrastructure, virtual machines, containers, serverless applications, industrial systems, and embedded devices.
Each architecture creates different advantages, limitations, responsibilities, and security concerns. Security+ expects you to recognize both the architecture and the tradeoff created by choosing it.
Use this sequence: architecture model, security implication, then business tradeoff.

entries.title: Architecture and Infrastructure Concepts
paragraphs: Architecture describes how computing environments and their supporting systems are designed and connected. Infrastructure is the collection of resources that makes that design operate.
entries.recognitionCue: Identify the design first, then identify the security consequence of using it.

sections.callout: Do not ask only, 'What architecture is this?' Also ask, 'What security consequence comes with choosing it?'

sections.title: Cloud
paragraphs: Cloud computing provides servers, storage, applications, networking, databases, and other computing resources through an external cloud environment.
Cloud can improve scalability and deployment speed, but moving a workload does not make security responsibility disappear.

entries.title: Cloud
paragraphs: The provider hosts the computing resources and delivers them as services over a network.
entries.memoryHook: The infrastructure moved; responsibility did not vanish.
entries.recognitionCue: Provider-hosted computing resources delivered as services -> Cloud

sections.title: Responsibility Matrix
paragraphs: A responsibility matrix identifies which cloud security duties belong to the provider and which belong to the customer. The division changes with the service model.

entries.title: Responsibility Matrix
paragraphs: The matrix may assign responsibility for physical infrastructure, operating systems, applications, data, identities, and configuration.
entries.recognitionCue: Determine whether provider or customer owns a security duty -> Responsibility matrix

sections.title: Hybrid and Third-Party Considerations
paragraphs: Cloud decisions can connect the organization to both its own infrastructure and outside providers. Security must cover those boundaries and dependencies.

entries.title: Hybrid Considerations
paragraphs: A hybrid environment combines cloud resources with infrastructure that remains on premises. Identity, connectivity, access controls, monitoring, and data movement must work securely across both environments.
entries.memoryHook: Two environments must behave like one secure environment.
entries.recognitionCue: Cloud plus on-premises infrastructure -> Hybrid considerations

entries.title: Third-Party Vendors
paragraphs: Outside vendors may store data, operate infrastructure, provide applications, or manage services. The organization becomes dependent on the vendor's security, availability, recovery, patching, and continuity.
entries.recognitionCue: Security or availability depends on an outside provider -> Third-party vendor consideration

sections.title: Infrastructure as Code and Serverless
paragraphs: Both models increase automation, but neither removes the need for secure configuration, permissions, application code, and data protection.

entries.title: Infrastructure as Code (IaC)
paragraphs: IaC uses machine-readable code or configuration files to define and deploy infrastructure consistently. It supports automation and reduces drift, but one insecure template can reproduce the same weakness many times.
entries.memoryHook: Automate the infrastructure, but secure the template.
entries.recognitionCue: Infrastructure created and configured through code -> IaC

entries.title: Serverless
paragraphs: Serverless computing lets customers run applications or event-driven functions without directly managing the underlying servers. Servers still exist; the provider manages much of that infrastructure while the customer remains responsible for code, permissions, data, and APIs.
entries.memoryHook: No server management does not mean no servers.
entries.recognitionCue: Provider manages the servers while the customer runs code -> Serverless

sections.title: Microservices
paragraphs: A microservices architecture divides an application into smaller independent services. Each service performs a function and communicates with other services.

entries.title: Microservices
paragraphs: Independent deployment and scaling can improve flexibility, but more services also create more APIs, authentication relationships, and service-to-service communication to secure.
entries.memoryHook: One large application becomes many smaller services.
entries.recognitionCue: Application divided into small independently deployable services -> Microservices

sections.title: Network Infrastructure
paragraphs: Network infrastructure includes the routers, switches, links, and supporting systems that provide connectivity. Its design controls how systems communicate and how strongly they are separated.

entries.title: Network Infrastructure
paragraphs: Security implications include physical isolation, air gaps, logical segmentation, and software-defined networking.
entries.recognitionCue: Connectivity and separation provided by network systems -> Network infrastructure

sections.title: Physical Isolation and Air Gaps
paragraphs: Physical separation removes a direct physical connection between environments. An air-gapped system has no normal network path to other networks.

entries.title: Physical Isolation
paragraphs: Physical isolation separates systems by preventing them from sharing a direct physical connection.
entries.recognitionCue: Separation created by physical infrastructure -> Physical isolation

entries.title: Air-Gapped
paragraphs: An air gap reduces remote attack exposure, but removable media and physical access can still introduce risk.
entries.memoryHook: No cable, no Wi-Fi, no normal network path.
entries.recognitionCue: Deliberately disconnected from normal networks -> Air-gapped

sections.title: Logical Segmentation and SDN
paragraphs: Logical controls can separate traffic and centrally direct network behavior while still using shared physical infrastructure.

entries.title: Logical Segmentation
paragraphs: Logical segmentation uses VLANs, network zones, access-control rules, or similar configuration to separate traffic.
entries.recognitionCue: Network separated through configuration -> Logical segmentation

entries.title: Software-Defined Networking (SDN)
paragraphs: SDN uses centralized software-based control to manage network policies and forwarding behavior. It can improve automation and change speed, while making the control plane an important security dependency.
entries.memoryHook: Software tells the network how to behave.
entries.recognitionCue: Programmable centralized control of network behavior -> SDN

table.caption: Physical and logical network separation
rows: Controlled network paths on shared infrastructure

sections.title: On-Premises
paragraphs: On-premises infrastructure is owned or directly operated by the organization in its own environment.

entries.title: On-Premises
paragraphs: The organization gains direct control while also accepting direct responsibility for servers, networking, storage, physical security, power, cooling, and patching.
entries.memoryHook: More direct control means more direct responsibility.
entries.recognitionCue: Organization directly operates infrastructure in its facilities -> On-premises

sections.title: Centralized and Decentralized Architecture
paragraphs: The placement of control changes management consistency, independence, and dependence on individual components.

entries.title: Centralized vs. Decentralized
paragraphs: A centralized architecture concentrates control or resources in one location or management system. This can simplify policy and monitoring but increases dependence on the central component.
A decentralized architecture distributes control across systems or locations. This reduces reliance on one central point but can make policy consistency, management, and monitoring more difficult.
entries.memoryHook: Centralized means one brain; decentralized means many brains.
entries.recognitionCue: One control point versus distributed control -> Centralized vs. decentralized

table.caption: Centralized and decentralized tradeoffs
rows: Consistent management with greater dependence on the central system
Greater local independence with more complex coordination

sections.title: Containers and Virtual Machines
paragraphs: Containers and virtual machines both isolate workloads, but they provide that isolation differently.

entries.title: Containerization
paragraphs: Containers package applications into lightweight isolated environments that generally share the host operating-system kernel. Security depends on images, configuration, permissions, and the host kernel.
entries.recognitionCue: Isolated application package sharing host OS resources -> Containerization

entries.title: Virtualization
paragraphs: Virtualization uses a hypervisor to run multiple virtual machines on one physical host. Each VM commonly includes its own guest operating system, applications, and virtual hardware.
entries.memoryHook: Several virtual computers on one physical machine.
entries.recognitionCue: Multiple guest systems managed through a hypervisor -> Virtualization

table.caption: Container and virtual-machine distinction
rows: Generally shares the host OS kernel
Generally has its own guest operating system

sections.title: Internet of Things
paragraphs: Internet of Things devices are network-connected, purpose-built devices such as cameras, sensors, smart devices, and building controllers.

entries.title: Internet of Things (IoT)
paragraphs: IoT devices may have limited computing power, weak default configurations, long lifecycles, and limited patch support.
entries.recognitionCue: Specialized network-connected device -> IoT

sections.title: ICS and SCADA
paragraphs: Industrial systems can affect manufacturing, utilities, energy, and physical processes, so a cybersecurity incident may create physical consequences.

entries.title: Industrial Control Systems (ICS)/SCADA
paragraphs: ICS controls or monitors industrial processes. SCADA provides central supervision, data collection, and operator control over industrial equipment.
entries.memoryHook: ICS controls the process; SCADA supervises the industrial environment.
entries.recognitionCue: Technology monitoring or controlling industrial processes -> ICS/SCADA

sections.title: RTOS and Embedded Systems
paragraphs: Specialized systems often operate with limited resources, long lifecycles, difficult patching, or strict timing requirements.

entries.title: Real-Time Operating System (RTOS)
paragraphs: An RTOS responds to events within predictable timing requirements. In these environments, an answer must be correct and arrive on time.
entries.recognitionCue: Strict, predictable response timing -> RTOS

entries.title: Embedded Systems
paragraphs: An embedded system is a computer built into another device for a specific function, such as a vehicle, appliance, medical device, or industrial machine. An IoT device may contain an embedded system, but embedded does not automatically mean network-connected.
entries.recognitionCue: Computer built into another device for a specific function -> Embedded system

sections.title: High Availability
paragraphs: High availability is designed to keep systems and services accessible with minimal interruption.

entries.title: High Availability
paragraphs: Redundancy, failover, clustering, and load balancing can allow service to continue when a component fails.
entries.memoryHook: One component fails, but the service keeps going.
entries.recognitionCue: Redundancy designed to minimize downtime -> High availability

sections.title: Architecture Considerations
paragraphs: Security+ may describe an architecture and ask about its operational or business tradeoff rather than asking for the technology name.

entries.title: Considerations
paragraphs: Architecture decisions must balance security, availability, resilience, cost, responsiveness, scalability, deployment, risk, recovery, patching, power, and compute.
entries.recognitionCue: Collective operational and business factors used to choose an architecture -> Considerations

sections.title: Availability and Resilience
paragraphs: Availability and resilience are related, but they answer different questions.

entries.title: Availability
paragraphs: Availability means authorized users can access systems and data when needed.
entries.recognitionCue: Can authorized users access the service? -> Availability

entries.title: Resilience
paragraphs: Resilience is the ability to withstand disruption and continue operating or recover.
entries.recognitionCue: Withstand or recover from disruption -> Resilience

sections.title: Cost, Responsiveness, Scalability, and Deployment
paragraphs: An architecture must satisfy business requirements as well as technical security requirements.

entries.title: Cost
paragraphs: Cost includes the financial impact of hardware, licensing, staffing, cloud charges, maintenance, and support.
entries.recognitionCue: Financial impact of an architecture -> Cost

entries.title: Responsiveness
paragraphs: Responsiveness describes how quickly a system reacts to requests or events. Latency can reduce responsiveness.
entries.recognitionCue: How quickly the system reacts -> Responsiveness

entries.title: Scalability
paragraphs: Scalability is the ability to increase or decrease capacity as demand changes.
entries.memoryHook: Can it grow when demand grows?
entries.recognitionCue: Add or remove capacity as demand changes -> Scalability

entries.title: Ease of Deployment
paragraphs: Cloud platforms, IaC, containers, and other models can make systems faster or more consistent to deploy.
entries.recognitionCue: How simply and quickly a solution can be placed into service -> Ease of deployment

sections.title: Risk, Recovery, and Patching
paragraphs: Architecture choices affect who accepts risk, how easily systems recover, and whether security fixes can be used.

entries.title: Risk Transference
paragraphs: Risk transference moves some financial or operational risk to another party through contracts, insurance, or third-party services. The risk does not disappear.
entries.memoryHook: Someone else accepts part of the risk.
entries.recognitionCue: Shift specified risk to another party -> Risk transference

entries.title: Ease of Recovery
paragraphs: Redundancy, backups, replicas, and automated deployment can make an environment easier to restore after disruption.
entries.recognitionCue: How readily a system can be restored -> Ease of recovery

entries.title: Patch Availability
paragraphs: Patch availability asks whether a vendor or provider has released a fix for a discovered weakness.
entries.recognitionCue: A vendor security fix exists -> Patch availability

entries.title: Inability to Patch
paragraphs: A patch may exist but be unsafe to apply because of legacy dependencies, compatibility, industrial requirements, or downtime restrictions. Compensating controls may be necessary.
entries.memoryHook: The fix exists, but the environment cannot safely install it.
entries.recognitionCue: Update cannot be applied without unacceptable impact -> Inability to patch

sections.title: Power and Compute
paragraphs: Architecture planning must provide the physical and processing resources required by the workload.

entries.title: Power
paragraphs: Power considerations include electrical capacity, redundancy, and backup power.
entries.recognitionCue: Electrical capacity and continuity requirements -> Power

entries.title: Compute
paragraphs: Compute refers to processing resources such as CPU and memory. The architecture must provide enough compute capacity for its workloads.
entries.recognitionCue: Processing and memory capacity required by workloads -> Compute

sections.title: Recognition Cues
paragraphs: Identify the architecture first, then identify the responsibility, limitation, or business tradeoff the scenario is testing.
bullets: Provider and customer duty split -> Responsibility matrix
Provider manages servers beneath customer code -> Serverless
Application divided into smaller services -> Microservices
No normal network path -> Air gap
Complete guest operating system -> Virtual machine
Computer inside another device -> Embedded system
Redundancy keeps service operating -> High availability
Withstand or recover from disruption -> Resilience
Risk shifted to another party -> Risk transference
Fix cannot safely be installed -> Inability to patch

sections.title: Objective 3.1 Exam Trap
paragraphs: Serverless does not mean no servers exist. It means the customer does not directly manage the underlying servers.
Containers generally share the host OS kernel. Virtual machines generally have their own guest operating systems.
An air gap is physical separation with no normal network path. Logical segmentation creates controlled separation through configuration.
Hybrid means cloud plus on-premises infrastructure. Multi-cloud means using multiple cloud providers and is a different concept.
Patch availability asks whether a fix exists. Inability to patch means the fix may exist but cannot be safely applied.
Availability asks whether the service is accessible. Resilience asks whether it can withstand disruption or recover.
sections.callout: Choose the architecture that fits the requirement, then verify that its security and business tradeoff also fits.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
paragraphs: Use this final sheet to connect each clue to its most direct architecture model or consideration.
bullets: Computer inside another device -> Embedded system
Cannot apply the fix -> Inability to patch

miniCheck.intro: Identify both the architecture and the cloud-governance tool described by the scenario.
miniCheck.prompt: An organization keeps a regulated database in its own data center but runs a customer application in a public cloud. Its design document separately identifies which security duties belong to the cloud provider and which belong to the customer.
miniCheck.correctFeedback: Correct. Combining an on-premises database with a public-cloud application creates a hybrid environment, while the responsibility matrix identifies which security duties belong to the provider and the customer.
miniCheck.retryFeedback: Not quite. First identify the model that combines cloud and on-premises resources. Then identify the document that answers, 'Who secures what?' Review Hybrid Considerations and the Responsibility Matrix, then try again.
